learning_objective: 🎯 Master the laws of heat and work! Understand how heat engines power our world, why refrigerators work, and why perfect efficiency is physically impossible.

main_concepts.concept_title: ⚖️ Zeroth and First Law of Thermodynamics
main_concepts.simple_explanation: The Zeroth law defines temperature: if A and B are in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in equilibrium with each other. The First Law is simply conservation of energy: Heat given to a system ($\Delta Q$) goes into changing its internal energy ($\Delta U$) and doing external work ($\Delta W$).

1. Isothermal: Temperature stays constant (slow process). 2. Adiabatic: No heat enters or leaves the system (very fast process, like a bursting tire). 3. Isochoric: Volume is constant (Work = 0). 4. Isobaric: Pressure is constant.

A heat engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, uses some of it to do mechanical work, and dumps the rest into a cold sink. A refrigerator is just a heat engine running in reverse—it takes work to pull heat out of a cold space and dump it into a hot room!

Heat always flows naturally from hot to cold, never the reverse. Kelvin-Planck statement: You can never build an engine that is 100% efficient (some heat is always wasted as exhaust). Clausius statement: You cannot move heat from cold to hot without doing external work.

A theoretical, idealized engine that operates on the Carnot cycle (reversible isothermal and adiabatic processes). It has the absolute maximum possible efficiency between two temperatures: $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_2}{T_1}$.

fun_activity.title: 🚲 The Bicycle Pump Heating
fun_activity.instructions: Take a manual bicycle pump and pump up a tire rapidly. Feel the bottom of the pump cylinder—it gets really hot! Because you compressed the air so fast, heat couldn't escape. This is a real-life 'Adiabatic Compression', which increases the internal energy (and thus temperature) of the gas!

exam_tips: 📌 Derivations for the work done in Isothermal ($W = nRT \ln(V_2/V_1)$) and Adiabatic ($W = \frac{nR(T_1 - T_2)}{\gamma - 1}$) processes are extremely important.
📌 Always use Absolute Temperature (Kelvin) when calculating Carnot engine efficiency.
📌 Be careful with the sign convention in the First Law: Heat added to the system is positive, and Work done BY the system (expansion) is positive.
quick_recap: ⭐ The First Law tells you that energy is conserved; the Second Law tells you which direction the energy will flow.
⭐ In an Isothermal process, the change in internal energy ($\Delta U$) of an ideal gas is exactly zero.
⭐ No real engine can ever be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures.
